summary: Dockerless is a trained Qwen3.5-9B patch verifier that judges an agent's candidate patch without running tests. It generates 2-4 verification questions from the issue and the reference (gold) patch, sends read-only grep/find sub-agents to gather repository evidence, then outputs a correctness score. Used as both the SFT trajectory filter and the RL reward, it produces a 9B SWE model that roughly matches environment-based post-training on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual and Pro.

claims.claim: Dockerless outperforms the strongest open-source verifier by 14.3 AUC points.
claims.evidence: Table 2: 81.0 vs DeepSWE Verifier 66.7 on the Verified split (776-sample balanced benchmark, 500 Verified + 276 Multi-SWE-bench Flash); +9.2 on Multi-SWE; +5.1 / +8.2 over the best zero-shot frontier judge. Single run, no CIs. Fig. 5 shows K=0 (no exploration) already reaches 78.3, so most of the gain over baselines comes from training plus reference-patch conditioning, not agentic exploration (+2.7).

claims.claim: The fully env-free pipeline reaches 62.0/50.0/35.2 on SWE-bench Verified/Multilingual/Pro, +2.4/+8.7/+2.9 over Qwen3.5-9B.
claims.evidence: Table 1 matches the abstract exactly. Gains over the base are small on Verified/Pro and come from one training run each with no seeds or variance. The '+20.8 over SWE-Lego-8B' comparison is against older, weaker backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Qwen3-8B).

Table 1/3: Dockerless-SFT 60.6/47.7/35.3 vs Env-SFT 60.0/48.3/33.9; Dockerless-RL 62.0/50.0/35.2 vs Test-Execution RL 62.4/51.3/35.7. Differences are within plausible run-to-run noise, but no variance is reported. Appendix E concedes a 7-13 point gap on compile-heavy languages (Rust +7.0, C +13.3 in favor of env-based).

claims.claim: Dockerless reward adds only 7.2% of per-rollout time in RL.
claims.evidence: §4.5 Fig. 6 over 7,680 rollouts: rollout 2,308 s mean, reward 41-180 s; Appendix F distributions overlap.

patterns.note: A trained, repository-exploring LLM verifier beats zero-shot frontier judges and prior trained verifiers in AUC, but it needs a gold reference patch, so it is not usable as a runtime reviewer of novel changes.
Execution-based reward still slightly wins (62.4 vs 62.0 Verified; 51.3 vs 50.0 Multilingual), and the value of a compiler/environment is concentrated in compile-heavy languages (Appendix E).
Parallel read-only sub-agents per verification question raise AUC from 78.3 (K=0) to 81.0 (K=4); gains plateau or fluctuate beyond 4.
Verifier-filtered SFT (top 4K of 16K) beats random 4K and the full 16K; GRPO with the verifier reward beats the DeepSWE-Verifier reward by 1.1-2.7 points.

methodology.sample: Verifier trained on 3.7K issues (SWE-Gym, Multi-SWE-RL); verifier eval 776 balanced trajectories; 16K env-free rollouts from SWE-Rebench-v2; resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified (500), Multilingual and Pro.
methodology.baselines: 4 zero-shot frontier judges (DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2.5, GLM-5, GPT-5.4) and 4 trained verifiers: reasonably current. The agent comparisons to SWE-Gym-7B/SWE-Dev-7B/SWE-Lego-8B use older backbones; the fair comparison is the Qwen3.5-9B base and the controlled env-based rows.
methodology.models: Single backbone (Qwen3.5-9B) for verifier and policy; GLM-5 as teacher.
methodology.variance: None reported; single training runs; differences of 0.4-1.4 points interpreted as 'matching'.
methodology.ablations: Filter source (Table 3), number of questions K (Fig. 5), reward source (Table 1).
methodology.contamination_controls: Training data stated disjoint from the verifier eval benchmark (C.1); no discussion of base-model pretraining contamination on SWE-bench Verified.
methodology.languages: Python-heavy Verified plus Multilingual/Pro (Go, JS, TS, Java, PHP, Rust, C, C++); per-language breakdown in Appendix E.

standards.artifacts: Prompts in Appendix G and hyperparameters in Appendix D; no code, model or data release URL found in the text.

biases.detail: 'Matches env-based' rests on sub-1.5-point differences from single runs.
Only Qwen3.5-9B is tested as verifier and policy backbone.

The verifier requires the golden reference patch, so the AUC measures 'equivalence to a known fix', not the ability to verify unknown changes; the title 'program verifier for coding agents' oversells it for runtime use.
All agent results are SWE-bench-family under one scaffold (OpenHands, 150 turns).
No repository or model weights linked.
The compile-heavy-language gap appears only in Appendix E.

verdict_reason: Solid controlled comparisons (filter source, reward source, number of questions) with abstract numbers matching Tables 1-2. However, results are single-run on one backbone, there is no code release, and the verifier depends on gold reference patches, which limits it to training-data curation rather than harness-time verification.
applicability: Mostly relevant to teams post-training their own coding models, which a Java backend content team is not. Two transferable lessons: (1) Appendix E shows that the compiler/build environment is where execution feedback matters most. For Java, keep `mvn compile`/tests in the agent loop rather than going env-free. (2) Read-only grep sub-agents that answer targeted verification questions are a cheap review aid across the ≥4 ingestion repos, but only when there is a reference behavior or spec to check against. In a spec-driven workflow the spec and acceptance criteria could play the role of the 'reference patch'; this is untested here.
